summary: This standards-track memo describes using AES in Galois/Counter Mode with IPsec ESP to provide both confidentiality and data origin authentication. It can be implemented efficiently in hardware for very high speeds.

plainLanguage.summary: GCM is a way of encrypting a packet that also proves where it came from, in a single pass over the data, so it can run at the speed of a fast link. This RFC describes how to use it inside IPsec, including the rules about never repeating a nonce with the same key.

questions: how to use gcm with ipsec
how does gcm work with esp
what is the nonce format for aes-gcm esp
what icv lengths does aes-gcm esp allow
subtitle: How IPsec ESP can encrypt and authenticate a packet in one pass, at 10 gigabits per second and above.

tldr.problem: ESP could use counter mode for speed, but counter mode on its own cannot prove that a packet really came from the sender, and none of the separate authentication methods could keep up with it at high data rates.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies AES in Galois/Counter Mode, which encrypts with a counter and computes an authentication tag at the same time. Each packet carries an 8-octet initialization vector, and the ESP header fields are covered by the tag without being encrypted.
tldr.outcome: The RFC assigned the transform identifiers 18, 19 and 20 that let two ends negotiate AES-GCM with different lengths of integrity check value.

facts.label: Nonce length
facts.value: 12 octets: a 4-octet salt plus the 8-octet IV

facts.label: Allowed ICV lengths
facts.value: 16 octets must be supported; 8 or 12 may be

facts.label: Key refresh limit
facts.value: A fresh key before encrypting 2^64 blocks

today: RFC 4106 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It specifies AES-GCM for IPsec ESP and assigns the transform identifiers used to negotiate it.

sections.title: Why Galois/Counter Mode
sections.content:
Counter mode has emerged as the preferred encryption method for high-speed implementations. Unlike conventional modes such as Cipher Block Chaining and CBC Message Authentication Code, counter mode can be implemented efficiently at high data rates because it can be pipelined. The ESP counter mode protocol describes how that mode can be used with IPsec ESP.

The problem with counter mode is that it provides no data origin authentication, so the ESP counter mode standard requires a separate data origin authentication algorithm alongside it. That requirement is problematic, because none of the standard data origin authentication algorithms can be implemented efficiently at high data rates. GCM solves it: underneath, it combines counter mode with a secure, parallelizable and efficient authentication mechanism.

The result is a mechanism that is efficient and secure and that also enables high-speed implementations in hardware, so that IPsec connections can make effective use of emerging 10-gigabit and 40-gigabit network devices. The RFC does not cover the implementation details of GCM itself, which are in the GCM specification along with test vectors.

The design was meant to be as similar as reasonable to the AES-CCM and AES-CTR ESP mechanisms, so that the experience with those standards could be reused. The main difference from CCM is the nonce length: the CCM ESP mechanism requires an 11-octet nonce, while GCM ESP uses a 12-octet nonce, and GCM is specially optimized to handle that case efficiently. Nonces of other lengths would cause unnecessary extra complexity and delay, particularly in hardware.
sections.plainLanguage: Counter mode is fast because the work on one block does not depend on the block before it. On its own it cannot show that a packet really came from the sender, and the usual ways of checking that were too slow to keep up. GCM does both at once.

sections.title: What GCM Does
sections.content:
GCM is a block cipher mode of operation that provides both confidentiality and data origin authentication. The authenticated encryption operation has four inputs: a secret key, an initialization vector, a plaintext, and an input for additional authenticated data, known as the AAD. It has two outputs: a ciphertext whose length is identical to the plaintext, and an authentication tag.

ESP also defines an initialization vector of its own. To keep the two apart, the RFC calls the GCM initialization vector a nonce in the context of AES-GCM-ESP. The same nonce and key combination must not be used more than once.

Because reusing a nonce and key combination destroys the security guarantees of AES-GCM, it can be difficult to use the mode securely with statically configured keys. For safety's sake, implementations must use an automated key management system, such as the Internet Key Exchange, to make sure the requirement is met.
sections.plainLanguage: GCM takes a key, a nonce, the text to protect and some extra data that should be checked but left readable. It returns the encrypted text, which is the same length as the input, plus a tag that proves both the text and the extra data were not altered.

sections.title: The ESP Payload
sections.content:
The ESP payload data is an eight-octet initialization vector followed by the ciphertext. The initialization vector field must be eight octets, and for a given key it must not repeat. The most natural way to implement this is with a counter, but anything that guarantees uniqueness can be used, such as a linear feedback shift register. The encrypter can use any IV generation method that meets the uniqueness requirement, without coordinating with the decrypter.

The plaintext given to AES-GCM is the plaintext data described by the Next Header field, concatenated with the padding, the pad length and the next header field itself. The ciphertext field holds the output of the AES-GCM algorithm, and its length is identical to that of the plaintext. Implementations that do not seek to hide the length of the plaintext should use the minimum amount of padding required, which will be less than four octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Each encrypted packet starts with eight bytes of counter value that must never repeat for the same key. After that comes the encrypted text, which is exactly as long as the text that was sent.

sections.title: The Nonce Format
sections.content: The nonce passed to the GCM-AES encryption algorithm has two parts. The salt is a four-octet value assigned at the beginning of the security association, and it then remains constant for the life of that security association. The salt should be unpredictable, meaning chosen at random, before it is selected, but it need not be secret. The second part is the initialization vector, which is the eight-octet field carried in the ESP payload. Together they make the 12-octet nonce that GCM is optimized for.
sections.plainLanguage: The nonce is split in two: four bytes that stay the same for the life of the connection, and eight bytes that change with every packet. Only the first part has to be secret, and it does not have to be.

sections.title: Protecting the ESP Header
sections.content:
The SPI and sequence number fields of the ESP header are authenticated for integrity and data origin without being encrypted. This is done by including those fields in the AES-GCM additional authenticated data field. Two formats of the AAD are defined: one for 32-bit sequence numbers, made up of the four-octet SPI followed by the four-octet sequence number, and one for 64-bit extended sequence numbers, where the eight-octet extended sequence number follows the SPI.

The effect is that a router can read the SPI and sequence number to decide where the packet should go and whether it is one it has already seen, while a change to either field is detected by the receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: The parts of the packet header that routers need in the clear are still protected: the receiver checks them along with the payload, so nobody can alter them in flight.

sections.title: The Integrity Check Value and Packet Growth
sections.content:
The integrity check value consists solely of the AES-GCM authentication tag. Implementations must support a full-length 16-octet ICV, may support 8 or 12 octet ICVs, and must not support other ICV lengths. Although ESP does not require an ICV to be present, AES-GCM-ESP deliberately does not allow a zero-length ICV, because GCM provides no integrity protection whatsoever when it is used with a zero-length authentication tag.

The packet grows in two places. The initialization vector adds eight octets, and the ICV adds 8, 12 or 16 octets. These are the only sources of packet expansion, other than the 10 to 13 octets taken up by the ESP SPI, sequence number, padding, pad length and next header fields when the minimum amount of padding is used.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver needs a tag to check the packet, and the RFC insists on at least a short one, because a tag of no length at all checks nothing. Each packet therefore grows by eight bytes for the counter and by the length of the tag.

sections.title: Agreeing on AES-GCM with IKE
sections.content:
This section sets out how the keying material and the salt are derived when the Internet Key Exchange is used, and the identifiers needed to negotiate a security association.

IKE uses a pseudo-random function to derive keying material, called KEYMAT, iteratively and without regard to the boundaries of the pieces it produces. The size of the KEYMAT for AES-GCM-ESP must be four octets longer than is needed for the associated AES key. With a 128-bit key, 20 octets are requested: the first 16 are the AES key and the remaining four are the salt value in the nonce. With a 192-bit key, 28 octets are requested, the first 24 being the key. With a 256-bit key, 36 octets are requested, the first 32 being the key. In each case the last four octets are the salt.

This document does not specify the conventions for using AES-GCM in IKE Phase 1 negotiations; for that, a separate specification and an Encryption Algorithm Identifier are needed. Implementations should use an IKE Phase 1 cipher at least as strong as AES-GCM, and the use of AES CBC with the same key size used by AES-GCM-ESP is recommended.

For IKE Phase 2 negotiations, IANA has assigned three ESP Transform Identifiers for AES-GCM with an eight-byte explicit IV: 18 for AES-GCM with an 8 octet ICV, 19 for AES-GCM with a 12 octet ICV, and 20 for AES-GCM with a 16 octet ICV. Because AES supports three key lengths, the Key Length attribute must be specified in the IKE Phase 2 exchange, and it must have a value of 128, 192 or 256.
sections.plainLanguage: The key exchange has to hand out enough key material for the cipher key and for the four bytes of salt, and the two ends have to agree on the numbers that stand for the cipher and for the length of the tag.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
GCM is provably secure against adversaries who can adaptively choose plaintexts, ciphertexts, ICVs and the AAD field, under standard cryptographic assumptions. In practice this means that, if it is used within its intended parameters, a break of GCM implies a break of the underlying block cipher.

The most important consideration is that the initialization vector must never repeat for a given key. Part of this is handled by disallowing the use of AES-GCM with statically configured keys. When IKE is used to establish fresh keys between two peers, separate keys are established for the two traffic flows. If some other mechanism is used that establishes only a single key for encrypting packets, there is a high probability that the peers will pick the same IV values for some packets, so implementations that allow the same key to be used for encrypting and decrypting packets with the same peer must ensure that the two peers assign different salt values to the security association.

The other consideration is that, as with any encryption mode, the security of all data protected under a given security association decreases slightly with each message. Implementations must generate a fresh key before encrypting 2^64 blocks of data with a given key. That limit is impossible to reach when using 32-bit sequence numbers.

For each message, GCM calls the block cipher once for each full 16-octet block in the payload, once for any remaining octets in the payload, and one additional time for computing the ICV. Smaller ICV values are more likely to be subject to forgery attacks, so implementations should use as large a size as is reasonable.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule that matters is simple: never use the same key with the same counter value twice, because that breaks the encryption. That is why the RFC insists on automatic key management and on a different salt for each direction of the connection.
